sources.title: Nikolay Przhevalsky (Q192442), verified live via the Wikidata API (2026-10-31): label 'Nikolay Przhevalsky', description 'Russian soldier, explorer, & geographer (1839-1888)', born 1839-03-31, died 1888-10-20 or 1888-11-01 (Old and New Style), citizenship Russian Empire, Korean label 니콜라이 프르제발스키. Orientation only; not used as support for any row.

Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Nikolay Przhevalsky' (full article read, about 5,000 characters). CANONICAL SIGNIFICANCE SOURCE: a Russian traveler who, by the extent of his explorations, route surveys and plant and animal collections, added vastly to geographic knowledge of east-central Asia; journeys from 1870 across Mongolia and the Gobi, to the Tien Shan, Takla Makan and Altun Mountains, to within 170 miles of Lhasa, and in 1883 to Ysyk-Kol; his natural history discoveries include the wild camel and Przewalski's horse; two travel books were translated into English; he died at Karakol.

EBSCO Research Starters, 'Przhevalsky Explores Central Asia' (read in full, about 7,500 words of article text). Modern reference summary of the four journeys of 1871-1885: the Qilian Shan and Choibseng base, the Lop Nur and Tarim basin, the third journey's wild-horse specimen, the survey of about three thousand miles and several tons of specimens, his dramatic travel writing, and the ill health that cut one expedition short. Also the counter-voice: it says the expeditions were partly meant to serve Russian expansion (a secondary aim never realised), that his contempt for the Chinese and Eurocentric, imperialist 1885 outline were repudiated by Russian policy makers, that Chekhov later revised his admiring view, and that rumours about his private life are unproven. Bibliography points to Rayfield's 'The Dream of Lhasa' (1976), which was not opened.

Colonel Henry Yule, 'Introductory Remarks' to N. Prejevalsky, 'Mongolia, the Tangut Country, and the Solitudes of Northern Tibet' (translated by E. Delmar Morgan; Sampson Low, London, 1876), read as the Internet Archive full-text scan of volume 1 (about 25 pages of the introduction). Contemporary independent assessment by the leading British authority on Asian geography: it places the journey against the state of knowledge of High Asia, calls Prejevalsky's exploration the boldest, most persevering and most extensive of the Russian incursions, says his narrative is accurate like a photograph but without much selection, retells the party's near-exhausted funds on the first journey, and records that Prejevalsky's attacks on the missionary Huc's narrative included two points where Prejevalsky was himself mistaken.

'Sketch of Nicholas Prejevalski', Popular Science Monthly, volume 30 (January 1887), read in full (about 4,000 words, Wikisource transcription). Contemporary periodical biography written while he was alive; it summarises the first three journeys with their instrument observations, collections and hardships, quotes his own narrative, reports that the geographer Petermann ranked the third journey very highly and that the Royal Geographical Society awarded him a gold medal in April 1879 with the quoted citation. Admiring and partly derived from his own books; the engraved portrait in this article is the portrait used here.

N. Prejevalsky, 'From Kulja, across the Tian Shan to Lob-Nor' (translated by E. Delmar Morgan; Sampson Low, London, 1879), Internet Archive full-text scan; read: the translator's preface, Baron von Richthofen's critique of the Lop Nur identification (the independent, adversarial voice), Prejevalsky's published replies, and sampled passages of his narrative (party composition, illness of a companion, hunting and collecting). The narrative and the replies are SELF-REPORT; Richthofen's critique is an independent expert challenge to his interpretation of the lake, though not of his observations.

Encyclopaedia Britannica, eleventh edition (1911), 'Prjevalsky, Nikolai Mikhailovich' (Wikisource transcription; read in full, about 600 words). Older reference biography with the career in order: Smolensk gymnasium, infantry regiment, general staff academy, teaching at Warsaw, Irkutsk and the Usuri in 1867-69, the first journey of 1870-73 with three men and 'ridiculously small pecuniary resources', medals, the later journeys, the collections and the fifth expedition begun in 1888. Its collection totals are older figures and are not used.

Wikipedia, 'Nikolay Przhevalsky' (read; orientation only, never counted as a source and not used as support for any row). It was read to see the secondary scholarship cited for his reputation (critical writing by Brennecke and Schimmelpenninck van der Oye on his attitudes and imperial aims, which was not opened) and the list of honours.

persistence.rationale: [src_przhev_psm, src_przhev_eb1911, src_przhev_yule, src_przhev_ebsco, src_przhev_kulja | 1870-1888 | contemporary periodical + reference + independent contemporary expert + modern summary + translator] Several independent sources record repeated returns to the same goal. Popular Science Monthly says that on the first journey he turned back when funds ran out, obtained a new pass and outfit at Peking and went out again to reach the Kuku-Nor, and that, not satisfied with the results, he organised a better-prepared second expedition; it also reports a grave illness after the Lop Nur journey and the planning of a further journey after recovery. Britannica 1911 and EBSCO count four journeys and a fifth begun in 1888 when he died; Yule (1876) calls his exploration the most persevering of the Russian incursions, and the translator Morgan (1879) cites his 'undaunted energy and perseverance'. The repeated failure to reach Lhasa is part of the same pattern. Most details come from his own reports as relayed, but the pattern is corroborated by non-self voices.

risk_tolerance.rationale: [src_przhev_eb1911, src_przhev_yule, src_przhev_psm, src_przhev_ebsco | 1870-1880 | reference + independent contemporary expert + periodical + modern summary] Britannica 1911 says the first journey was made with only three men and ridiculously small pecuniary resources; Yule reports that after buying camels about forty pounds remained and that, sure of maintenance from their guns, he resolved to push on; Popular Science Monthly describes the party near the end as half starved and ragged after crossing a stretch of the Ala-shan desert without a guide. EBSCO adds that his bravado and marksmanship at times served him well. Dual-edged because the thin outfit forced turn-backs on the first journey (Popular Science Monthly says he lamented its insufficiency) and the arrangement exposed his companions to the same hardship.

resourcefulness.rationale: [src_przhev_yule, src_przhev_psm, src_przhev_ebsco | 1870-1873 | independent contemporary expert + periodical + modern summary] With little money he lived largely from hunting while travelling (Yule), and Popular Science Monthly says that, despite lamenting an insufficient outfit, he carried a hand-compass route survey of about 3,300 miles, defined eighteen meridians and kept regular meteorological and magnetic observations; EBSCO says he gained standing with local people through his reputation as a marksman and through use of Western medicine and a barometer to predict weather. The evidence is of making a thin expedition work rather than of a documented inventive solution to a specific problem.

planning_orientation.rationale: [src_przhev_psm, src_przhev_kulja, src_przhev_eb1911 | 1873-1879 | periodical + self-report + reference] Popular Science Monthly says that after the first journey he organised a second expedition 'to be more adequately prepared', and it describes the third-journey party as twelve companions with specialised zoological and botanical staff, baggage in forty-six packages on twenty-three camels, and arms in which the whole company was carefully drilled; his own narrative lists the formation and equipment of the Kulja caravan over nearly three weeks. These details are largely his own reporting relayed by the periodical, so confidence stays moderate, and he also names failings in his choice of companions on the Lop Nur journey in his own narrative.

detail_orientation.rationale: [src_przhev_psm, src_przhev_yule, src_przhev_kulja | 1870-1879 | periodical + independent contemporary expert + critique and reply] Popular Science Monthly reports meteorological observations four times a day, frequent ground-temperature and hygrometric readings, magnetic observations at nine points and detailed ornithological and mammal collections on the first journey; Yule says his narrative is a careful, accurate picture 'like a photograph' though with little selection. Richthofen's critique accepts the observations but argues the identification of the Lop Nur lake was mistaken, and Prejevalsky's published reply defends his survey on the ground that he followed the river bank and saw no other channel. Yule also found two of Prejevalsky's corrections of Huc to be Prejevalsky's own errors, so the claim of care is not unqualified. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): reviewed as a top-risk row; lowered from 70 / 0.58 to 66 / 0.54 because the instrument-observation detail reaches us through his own reports relayed by an admiring periodical, and Yule shows at least two of his own factual corrections were wrong.

curiosity.rationale: [src_przhev_psm, src_przhev_kulja, src_przhev_ebsco, src_przhev_eb1911 | 1867-1880 | periodical + self-report + modern summary + reference] He took himself to Irkutsk at his own request in 1867 to explore the Usuri country (Popular Science Monthly says this region fixed the direction of his career), and his expeditions collected birds, mammals, insects, plants and minerals and recorded ethnography and physiography; Popular Science Monthly reports that Nature thought his Lop Nur notes on bird migration exceptionally valuable; EBSCO says he searched for a wild horse and for the fabled yeti, finding no authentic specimens of the latter. The signal is of wide-ranging field inquiry rather than abstract questioning, and the military framing of the journeys limits how far the motive can be read as pure curiosity.

portrait.source: Wood engraving of Nicholas Prejevalski published as the illustration to 'Sketch of Nicholas Prejevalski', Popular Science Monthly, volume 30 (January 1887), page 304 (plate D304), engraver not identified (a signature at lower left is illegible). Hosted on Wikimedia Commons as 'PSM V30 D304 Nicholas Prejevalsky.jpg' from the Internet Archive scan of the volume; I opened the Wikisource article that carries it. Rights basis: first published in the United States in 1887, so in the public domain in the United States by publication date regardless of the engraver; no institutional notice conflicts (the periodical's own pages are the source and carry no restriction). The Commons file page gives only a generic old-work tag, so the basis rests on the documented 1887 publication. Original scan 1759 x 2335 pixels, downscaled with no cropping to 904 x 1200; never upscaled. An engraving is a depiction made in his lifetime from an unstated source, not a documented sitting, so it is classed as a historical depiction like other engravings in this roster.
portrait.attribution: Engraving in Popular Science Monthly, vol. 30 (January 1887), via Wikimedia Commons (public domain)
portrait.creator: Unidentified engraver, in Popular Science Monthly

provenance.notes: portrait_preflight: plausible (lead) / PARTLY CONFIRMED, DIFFERENT FILE USED. The lead's Commons file 'Nikolay Przhevalsky photoportrait and signature.jpg' (628x789; credited 'V. Klasen', from the 1888 book 'Fourth Journey in Central Asia', St Petersburg) is a genuine period photograph, but the Commons page is only a one-line uploader attribution with a bare PD-US tag and I could not open the 1888 book to confirm that this portrait is printed in it or credited to Klasen, so it was not used (I verified only that the book exists, with phototypes, from catalogue listings). Used instead the 1887 wood engraving printed in Popular Science Monthly vol. 30, which I confirmed on the Wikisource article page; basis is publication date. READ: Britannica, EBSCO Research Starters (full), Yule's introduction in the 1876 English edition (about 25 pages), Popular Science Monthly 1887 (full), the 1879 'From Kulja' book (preface, Richthofen's critique, his replies, sampled narrative), Britannica 1911 (full), Wikipedia (orientation). PERSPECTIVES: modern reference summary, independent contemporary British expert, contemporary periodical, translator's preface, adversarial expert critique (Richthofen), self-report. COUNTER-VOICES: Richthofen's challenge to the Lop Nur identification (and Morgan's note that the criticism was premature), Yule's finding that two of Prejevalsky's corrections of Huc were mistaken, EBSCO's account of his chauvinism and the repudiated imperial outline, Chekhov's changed view as reported by EBSCO. NOT OPENED: Rayfield's 'The Dream of Lhasa', the Britannica 1911 numbers beyond the text read, the Russian-language biographies (Dubrovin), the Presidential Library page (bot check), the Columbia Tibetan culture chronology page (certificate error), Brennecke and Schimmelpenninck van der Oye (known only through Wikipedia's citations), Chekhov's own essay. SELF-REPORT SEPARATION: his own narrative and replies are self-report; planning, resourcefulness and curiosity rows rest on non-self periodical and reference accounts that largely derive from his books, which is why confidence is capped near 0.5. CONFLICT NOTED: the distance he came to Lhasa differs by source (Britannica 170 miles, EBSCO 26 miles, Popular Science Monthly about 500 miles on the first journey), so no distance is stated in the achievement cards.
